tip: For health and how you feel, use stare, not essere: sto bene = I'm well, literally I stay well.
Italian uses avere (have) where English uses be: ha torto = he's wrong, literally he has wrong.
Fear takes avere, not essere: ha paura = she's afraid, literally she has fear.
Put più before an adjective or adverb to say more: più forte = louder.
Names of languages take the definite article: studi l'italiano = you study Italian.
Bene is the adverb (well); buono is the adjective (good). Canta bene = sings well.
The present tense also covers the near future: parte stasera = he's leaving tonight.
Use stare plus an adjective for a temporary state: sta zitto = he keeps quiet.
Parere means to seem, an everyday match for sembrare: pare contento = he seems happy.
Unlike English, nationalities are written in lowercase: sono italiano = I am Italian.
È with an accent is the verb is; e without it means and: lui è alto = he is tall.
Adjectives ending in -e use one plural, -i, for both genders: felici.
Questions keep statement word order; only the rising tone changes: sei sicuro?
Being right takes avere: avere ragione = to be right, literally to have reason.
To make a verb negative, place non right before it: non ho capito = I didn't understand.
For an informal -are command, drop -re and end in -a: mangia = eat.
Informal commands from -ere and -ire verbs end in -i: chiudi = close.
Being in a hurry uses avere: abbiamo fretta = we're in a hurry, literally we have hurry.
Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, una drops to un': un'applicazione.
Many adjectives ending in -co add an h in the plural to keep the hard c sound: stanco becomes stanchi.
Origin uses di: Di dove sei? = where are you from, literally of where are you.
Cambiare idea means to change one's mind, with no possessive word added: cambiato idea.
Aspettare already means to wait for, so there is no separate word for for: aspettato un'ora.
A negative informal command is non plus the infinitive: non mangiare = don't eat.
The noi present form also means let's: mangiamo = let's eat.
Chi means whoever and always takes a singular verb: chi studia = those who study.
Prendere has the irregular past participle preso, not prenduto.
Reflexive verbs form the past with essere, so the participle agrees: si è sentito.
Fino a means up to or until: conto fino a dieci = I count to ten.
Tutto agrees and keeps the article after it: tutta la sera = the whole evening.
Grocery shopping is fare la spesa, built on fare, not comprare.
In an informal command the reflexive pronoun attaches to the end: ferma plus ti gives fermati.
Scorso means last in the sense of just past: il mese scorso = last month.
Leggere has the irregular past participle letto.
Rompere has the irregular past participle rotto.
Possession is shown with di: la macchina di sua madre = his mother's car.
Da plus l' contracts to dall': dall'ufficio = from the office.
Object pronouns attach to the end of an infinitive: chiamare plus ti gives chiamarti.
Quello shortens to quel before a masculine noun starting with a consonant: quel libro.
Magari plus the past subjunctive expresses a wish: magari parlassi = I wish I spoke.
Svegliarsi is reflexive, so it needs mi: mi sveglio = I wake up, literally I wake myself.
Vedere has the irregular past participle visto.
To visit a person use andare or venire a trovare; visitare is for places: venuta a trovarmi.
Come se (as if) always takes the subjunctive: come se sapesse = as if he knew.
Add -mente to an adjective to build an adverb: veloce becomes velocemente = quickly.
After a time phrase, fa means ago: poco fa = a little while ago.
Drop the article with a possessive before one singular family member: tua sorella = your sister.
